title: Closing the Null Space: Guidance-AwareQuantization for Classifier-Free Diffusion

paper.title: Closing the Null Space: Guidance-Aware Quantization for Classifier-Free Diffusion
paper.abstract:
Abstract Deploying classifier-free guidance (CFG) diffusion models under
real-world compute budgets requires quantization, yet existing
post-training quantization (PTQ) methods treat CFG models as
single-branch networks, ignoring the paired conditional/unconditional
structure that CFG inference fundamentally relies on.
This structural blind spot has two consequences.
At the system level, the two-pass CFG execution pattern imposes a
latency overhead that parameter-count and bit-operation metrics
conceal entirely, and commodity INT8 inference stacks fail to
realize the theoretical efficiency gains that BOPs calculations
promise.
At the algorithmic level, calibrating against the guidance gap
alone admits an exact null space: a quantized model can achieve
perfect gap-fidelity diagnostics while the unconditional branch
drifts arbitrarily, corrupting every guided prediction at inference
time.
This paper terms this the branch-drift trap , proves its
existence analytically, and confirms it empirically through a
false-positive result in which the best-calibrated model
by standard diagnostics simultaneously produces the worst sample
quality.
To close the trap, Guidance-Aware Mixed Precision (GAMP) is
proposed, which calibrates directly on the guided prediction,
derives per-layer activation-bit sensitivity from guided-output
degradation, and allocates bits via a greedy knapsack—provably
preventing unconditional branch drift by construction.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models [ 1 ] have become the dominant framework for high-quality conditional image generation, with classifier-free guidance (CFG) [ 2 ] providing the primary control mechanism at inference time. Deploying these models under memory and latency budgets motivates post-training quantization (PTQ), which compresses a trained model by quantizing its weights and activations without retraining. CFG inference, however, differs fundamentally from the unconditional generation setting that virtually all PTQ methods assume: at every denoising step, the model executes two forward passes—one conditioned on a class label and one on a null token—whose outputs are combined as 𝜺 ~ = 𝜺 ∅ + w ⁡ ( 𝜺 y − 𝜺 ∅ ) , w > 1 . \tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}+w(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{y}-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}),\quad w>1. (1) This dual-branch structure creates two deployment challenges that the existing PTQ literature has not addressed. The first is a measurement problem. Efficiency metrics such as parameter counts and bit-operations (BOPs) report single-pass costs, invisibly discounting the two-pass per-step overhead that CFG imposes. The same measurement gap affects INT8 deployment: BOPs-predicted speedups assume hardware-matched inference stacks, but commodity ONNX Runtime without TensorRT routes quantized operators through fallback pathways that negate—and in practice reverse—the theoretical gains. The second is a calibration problem, and it is structural. A natural PTQ objective for a CFG model is to calibrate the guidance gap 𝚫 = 𝜺 y − 𝜺 ∅ \boldsymbol{\Delta}=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{y}-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset} , since DASH’s distillation work [ 5 ] demonstrates that preserving 𝚫 \boldsymbol{\Delta} is central to generation quality. This paper shows, however, that a gap-only calibration objective admits an exact null space: there exist quantized models that achieve perfect gap fidelity—near-ideal ρ \rho and cos ⁡ ( 𝚫 ) \cos(\boldsymbol{\Delta}) scores—while the unconditional branch drifts by an unconstrained vector 𝜹 \boldsymbol{\delta} , corrupting the guided prediction at inference time. This phenomenon is termed the branch-drift trap . Unlike the training-time setting in DASH, where an explicit unconditional branch loss and hundreds of thousands of gradient steps over unfrozen weights close this null space automatically, PTQ calibrates only quantization thresholds over frozen weights in a few hundred iterations—a regime in which no gradient mechanism exists to suppress 𝜹 \boldsymbol{\delta} . To address both challenges, this paper makes four contributions. 1. CFG latency characterization : the two-pass guided-inference overhead is measured empirically on an NVIDIA T4 GPU across batch sizes and floating-point formats, revealing a consistent 1.99 × \times tax hidden by all standard efficiency proxies and diagnosing a precise software-stack root cause for the failure of commodity INT8 inference to realize theoretical speedups. 2. Null-space theorem and empirical confirmation : the branch-drift trap is proved formally—showing that gap-only PTQ calibration admits an exact null space in which guided-prediction error is unconstrained—and confirmed empirically through a controlled ablation in which the best-performing model by gap diagnostics simultaneously produces the worst sample quality of any tested configuration. 3. Guidance-Aware Mixed Precision (GAMP) : a PTQ method that calibrates on the guided prediction directly, closes the null space by construction, and allocates activation bits per layer according to their contribution to guided-output degradation—a CFG-aware sensitivity criterion that the existing single-branch mixed-precision literature does not capture. 4. Deployment guidelines : concrete recommendations for HPEC practitioners on how to report efficiency, validate PTQ calibration, and allocate activation precision for CFG diffusion deployment.

sections.heading: II Related Work
sections.text: Post-training quantization for diffusion models. PTQ4DM [ 14 ] established the feasibility of diffusion PTQ by collecting multi-timestep calibration data to address time-varying activation statistics. Q-Diffusion [ 8 ] introduced skip-connection partitioning and block-wise reconstruction; for text-conditioned models it collects features from both CFG branches, but its reconstruction objective is per-block MSE on each branch independently, not the guided prediction 𝜺 ~ = 𝜺 ∅ + w ​ 𝚫 \tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}+w\boldsymbol{\Delta} . PTQD [ 9 ] modeled quantization noise as a perturbation of the diffusion SDE, proposing timestep-aware mixed-precision that targets trajectory accumulation—a complementary error source to the branch-level failure identified here. TFMQ-DM [ 10 ] , APQ-DM [ 15 ] , and TCAQ-DM [ 16 ] introduced further refinements to temporal feature maintenance and per-channel calibration. Despite these advances, no existing method calibrates against 𝜺 ~ \tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}} directly: all treat the CFG model as a single-pass unconditional network during calibration, leaving the branch-drift trap structurally unaddressed. The failure mode is architecture-agnostic—it depends only on the linear combination in ( 1 ) and applies equally to convolutional UNets and transformer-based DiT architectures. Existing per-block MSE or per-tensor reconstruction losses, even when fed with dual-branch features, remain gap-like objectives in the terminal output space: they minimize branch-wise discrepancies independently. Because no explicit coupling term constrains 𝜹 \boldsymbol{\delta} , the null space of Proposition 1 remains reachable—a constant branch offset propagates through the network and achieves low per-block error on both branches simultaneously while severely corrupting 𝜺 ~ \tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}} . Mixed-precision allocation. BRECQ [ 7 ] and HAWQ [ 11 ] allocate bit-widths by per-layer sensitivity derived from block-wise reconstruction error or Hessian curvature—single-pass proxies that do not account for CFG’s dual-branch structure. GAMP instead measures sensitivity through ‖ 𝜺 ~ l q − 𝜺 ~ l f ​ p ‖ 2 \left\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}^{q}_{l}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}^{fp}_{l}\right\|^{2} , the quantity CFG sampling depends on directly, targeting the deployment-critical failure mode rather than a reconstruction proxy. CFG distillation and the DASH null space. DASH [ 5 ] compresses a 35.8M-parameter CFG teacher to a 6.1M student via distillation, introducing ρ \rho and cos ⁡ ( 𝚫 ) \cos(\boldsymbol{\Delta}) as guidance-fidelity diagnostics and proving a training-time null space for gap matching under full gradient access. The present work extends this analysis to the PTQ regime, where frozen weights make the null space provably impossible to escape via gap calibration alone, and demonstrates that the diagnostics DASH correctly uses for distillation monitoring become insufficient —and actively misleading—as PTQ calibration objectives.

sections.heading: III-A Preliminaries
sections.text: At each of K = 50 K\!=\!50 DDIM [ 3 ] steps, two forward passes through the UNet yield 𝜺 y ​ ( x t , t ) \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{y}(x_{t},t) (conditional, class label y y ) and 𝜺 ∅ ​ ( x t , t ) \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}(x_{t},t) (unconditional, null token), combined by ( 1 ). The guidance gap 𝚫 = 𝜺 y − 𝜺 ∅ \boldsymbol{\Delta}=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{y}-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset} carries the class signal; DASH [ 5 ] quantifies its preservation by ρ = 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ 𝚫 q ‖ ] / 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ 𝚫 f ​ p ‖ ] \rho\!=\!\mathbb{E}[\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{q}\|]/\mathbb{E}[\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{fp}\|] (magnitude ratio; ideal 1) and cos ⁡ ( 𝚫 q , 𝚫 f ​ p ) \cos(\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{q},\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{fp}) (directional alignment; ideal 1). Quantization thresholds are optimized via AdaRound-style [ 6 ] learnable weight rounding with MSE-optimal activation clipping, over 800 iterations using 1 024 calibration images drawn uniformly from the CIFAR-10 training set; network weights are frozen throughout. Weights are quantized per-output-channel (symmetric, signed), providing scale granularity that substantially reduces clipping error at W4; activations are quantized per-tensor (asymmetric, unsigned) with MSE-optimal clipping thresholds. Biases and normalization parameters remain at FP32. Bit-operations BOPs = ∑ l M l ​ w b ​ a b \text{BOPs}\!=\!\sum_{l}M_{l}w_{b}a_{b} ( M l M_{l} : layer MACs, w b w_{b} : weight bits, a b a_{b} : activation bits) serve as the hardware-agnostic compute metric. The first and last UNet convolutions ( conv_in , conv_out ) remain FP32, consistent with standard diffusion PTQ practice [ 8 ] .

sections.heading: III-B The Branch-Drift Trap: Null-Space Analysis
sections.text: The most natural PTQ calibration objective for a CFG model is to minimize the guidance-gap reconstruction error: ℒ gap = ‖ ( 𝜺 y q − 𝜺 ∅ q ) − ( 𝜺 y f ​ p − 𝜺 ∅ f ​ p ) ‖ 2 . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gap}}=\left\|(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{y}^{q}-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{q})-(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{y}^{fp}-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{fp})\right\|^{2}. (2) This is well-motivated: ℒ gap \mathcal{L}_{\text{gap}} directly penalizes drift in 𝚫 \boldsymbol{\Delta} , the quantity DASH identifies as the primary quality determinant. Proof. At each of the K K DDIM steps, Proposition 2 contributes ‖ 𝛅 ‖ \left\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\right\| of per-step error; over the full trajectory, ℓ 2 \ell_{2} error accumulates as 𝒪 ⁡ ( K ​ ‖ 𝛅 ‖ ) \mathcal{O}(K\left\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\right\|) . Guidance-gap metrics are necessary but not sufficient for PTQ sample quality under CFG. PTQ provides no mechanism to suppress this drift. In DASH’s distillation setting [ 5 ] , an explicit unconditional branch loss ℒ u ​ n = ‖ 𝜺 ∅ student − 𝜺 ∅ teacher ‖ 2 \mathcal{L}_{un}\!=\!\left\|\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{\text{student}}-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{\text{teacher}}\right\|^{2} applied over > > 200K gradient iterations on unfrozen weights directly suppresses 𝜹 \boldsymbol{\delta} . In PTQ, threshold optimization has only 𝒪 ⁡ ( L ) \mathcal{O}(L) degrees of freedom (one clipping range per quantizable layer), and the gap loss reaches ℒ gap ≈ 0 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gap}}\!\approx\!0 trivially by shifting both branch outputs by a common offset without genuinely aligning either branch to its full-precision reference. The branch-drift trap is therefore a structural property of any gap-only PTQ objective, not an optimization pathology. At larger guidance scales ( w ∼ 7 w\!\sim\!7 –15 in text-to-image generation), the guided-prediction magnitude grows as | 𝜺 ~ | ∝ w ​ ‖ 𝚫 ‖ |\tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}|\propto w\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\| while 𝜹 \boldsymbol{\delta} remains fixed in absolute magnitude by ( 3 ), making the drift a proportionally larger directional contamination of the sampling score. The branch-drift trap is therefore expected to intensify at production guidance scales. Propositions 1 – 2 jointly imply that the PTQ objective must constrain the guided prediction 𝜺 ~ = 𝜺 ∅ + w ​ 𝚫 \tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}+w\boldsymbol{\Delta} directly. GAMP uses ℰ ⁡ ( l ) \mathcal{E}(l) as both its per-layer sensitivity signal and the basis of its calibration objective.

sections.heading: IV-A Setup
sections.text: The branch-drift trap established in Propositions 1 and 2 is a structural algebraic consequence of ( 1 ), independent of dataset size, image resolution, or label-space cardinality: the null-space argument holds for any CFG model that evaluates two forward passes and combines them linearly. Likewise, the ONNX Runtime INT8 bottleneck (Section IV-C ) is governed by operator-mapping rules within the software stack, not by image content. CIFAR-10 therefore provides a sufficient and computationally controlled setting for isolating these structural and system-level behaviors without confounding data-scale variables. Model and data. The publicly released DASH student checkpoints [ 5 ] are used: a 6.1M-parameter ADM UNet [ 4 ] (base channels 64, one residual block per scale, attention at × 16 16\!\times\!16 ) trained on CIFAR-10, × 32 32\!\times\!32 RGB. FP32 evaluation on a single-seed 50k-sample protocol yields FID 13.67; the DASH paper reports 8.87 as a multi-seed mean from its own training pipeline. All PTQ comparisons use the same single-seed protocol; the single-seed variance ( ± \pm 2–3 FID at 50k samples) is small relative to the differences reported. Baselines. (i) RTN : round-to-nearest, no calibration; (ii) MSE-cal : AdaRound rounding with MSE activation clipping, dual-branch calibration, uniform precision; (iii) Gap-only : gap objective ( 2 ) as the sole calibration target—the critical ablation validating Corollary 1 ; (iv) GAMP (ours) at b ¯ ∈ { 5 , 6 } \bar{b}\!\in\!\{5,6\} average activation bits. Metrics. FID and IS (50k samples, torch-fidelity , cifar10-train reference) [ 12 , 13 ] ; guidance-gap diagnostics ρ \rho , cos ⁡ ( 𝚫 ) \cos(\boldsymbol{\Delta}) [ 5 ] ; BOPs per guided step ( = ⁣ × =\!2\!\times single-pass BOPs); theoretical packed model size (MB). Hardware. The NVIDIA T4 (16 GB) is chosen deliberately: as the most widely deployed cost-effective cloud and edge inference accelerator, it ensures the 147 × \times software-stack gap diagnosed in Section IV-C reflects conditions faced by budget-constrained practitioners, not an unusual hardware configuration. Timing uses PyTorch cuda.Event (20 reps, 8 warmup); INT8 measurements use ONNX Runtime 1.18 (CUDA EP, no TensorRT).

W8A8 single-pass BOPs predict a 16 × \times speedup over FP32; ORT INT8 without TensorRT delivers a single-pass latency of 4 598 ms against 31.2 ms for PyTorch FP16—a ≈ \approx 147 × \times slowdown (Fig. 3 ). The root cause is diagnosed as follows. TensorRT libraries are absent from the Kaggle T4 environment ( libnvinfer.so.10 not found ), preventing ONNX Runtime from dispatching quantized operators to the GPU’s INT8 tensor cores. As a result, the quantized ONNX graph contains 192 GPU ↔ \leftrightarrow CPU memcpy nodes (one per quantized operator), each incurring a PCIe round-trip; additionally, UNet downsample Slice operations resist dynamic INT8 quantization and execute at FP32 within the nominally INT8 graph. This is a software-stack finding, not a verdict on INT8 arithmetic: the 3.8 × 3.8\times disk-size reduction (6.4 vs. 24.5 MB) confirms weight quantization succeeds; the bottleneck is inference-stack support, not arithmetic capability. sections.heading: V Conclusion
sections.text: This paper characterizes post-training quantization of CFG diffusion models along three dimensions the existing literature has left unaddressed. Measured profiling on T4 confirms a consistent 1.99 × \times guided-inference overhead hidden by all standard efficiency metrics. A precise software-stack diagnosis isolates the 147 × \times INT8 slowdown to an operator-fallback artifact rather than an arithmetic limitation, clarifying that the BOPs-to-latency gap is a deployment-pipeline problem. The branch-drift trap—an exact null space in gap-only PTQ calibration, confirmed at ( cos ⁡ ( 𝚫 ) = 0.882 \cos(\boldsymbol{\Delta})\!=\!0.882 , FID 334)—is the paper’s central theoretical and empirical contribution. GAMP closes this trap by construction and allocates activation bits by guided-output sensitivity, achieving a 49% FID improvement over the uniform-spending reference at matched average precision ( b ¯ \bar{b} 6) and near-W4A8 quality at 13% fewer BOPs than the uniform W4A8 counterpart ( b ¯ \bar{b} 5). For HPEC practitioners, three guidelines follow: report guided-step BOPs; validate PTQ calibration with guided-prediction error rather than gap diagnostics alone; and allocate activation bits by GAMP sensitivity when the activation cliff falls within the compression regime. Limitations and future work. Experiments are restricted to × 32 32\!\times\!32 pixel-space diffusion (CIFAR-10) on a compact 6.1M student; validating GAMP on Stable Diffusion and similar latent CFG models, and on Hopper-generation accelerators (e.g., H100) where INT8 tensor-core support is more mature, is the primary scale-up direction. The branch-drift analysis predicts the trap intensifies with w w , motivating ablations at guidance scales w ∼ 7 w\!\sim\!7 –15 typical of text-to-image generation. Adding an unconditional anchor λ ​ ‖ 𝜺 ∅ q − 𝜺 ∅ f ​ p ‖ 2 \lambda\left\|\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{q}-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{fp}\right\|^{2} to ℒ gap \mathcal{L}_{\text{gap}} closes the null space provably and is the most direct methodological extension. Combining GAMP with PTQD-style per-step allocation is the primary algorithmic follow-up.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2607.08241v1 [cs.CV] 09 Jul 2026 Closing the Null Space: Guidance-Aware Quantization for Classifier-Free Diffusion Abdullah Al Shafi, Sumaiya Rahim Suma Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering Khulna University of Engineering & Technology Khulna-9203, Bangladesh {abdullah.shafi99, sumaiya.rahim234}@gmail.com Abstract Deploying classifier-free guidance (CFG) diffusion models under real-world compute budgets requires quantization, yet existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods treat CFG models as single-branch networks, ignoring the paired conditional/unconditional structure that CFG inference fundamentally relies on. This structural blind spot has two consequences. At the system level, the two-pass CFG execution pattern imposes a latency overhead that parameter-count and bit-operation metrics conceal entirely, and commodity INT8 inference stacks fail to realize the theoretical efficiency gains that BOPs calculations promise. At the algorithmic level, calibrating against the guidance gap alone admits an exact null space: a quantized model can achieve perfect gap-fidelity diagnostics while the unconditional branch drifts arbitrarily, corrupting every guided prediction at inference time. This paper terms this the branch-drift trap , proves its existence analytically, and confirms it empirically through a false-positive result in which the best-calibrated model by standard diagnostics simultaneously produces the worst sample quality. To close the trap, Guidance-Aware Mixed Precision (GAMP) is proposed, which calibrates directly on the guided prediction, derives per-layer activation-bit sensitivity from guided-output degradation, and allocates bits via a greedy knapsack—provably preventing unconditional branch drift by construction. Index Terms: post-training quantization, classifier-free guidance, diffusion models, mixed precision, branch-drift trap, null space, inference efficiency I Introduction Diffusion models [ 1 ] have become the dominant framework for high-quality conditional image generation, with classifier-free guidance (CFG) [ 2 ] providing the primary control mechanism at inference time. Deploying these models under memory and latency budgets motivates post-training quantization (PTQ), which compresses a trained model by quantizing its weights and activations without retraining. CFG inference, however, differs fundamentally from the unconditional generation setting that virtually all PTQ methods assume: at every denoising step, the model executes two forward passes—one conditioned on a class label and one on a null token—whose outputs are combined as 𝜺 ~ = 𝜺 ∅ + w ⁡ ( 𝜺 y − 𝜺 ∅ ) , w > 1 . \tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}+w(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{y}-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}),\quad w>1. (1) This dual-branch structure creates two deployment challenges that the existing PTQ literature has not addressed. The first is a measurement problem. Efficiency metrics such as parameter counts and bit-operations (BOPs) report single-pass costs, invisibly discounting the two-pass per-step overhead that CFG imposes. The same measurement gap affects INT8 deployment: BOPs-predicted speedups assume hardware-matched inference stacks, but commodity ONNX Runtime without TensorRT routes quantized operators through fallback pathways that negate—and in practice reverse—the theoretical gains. The second is a calibration problem, and it is structural. A natural PTQ objective for a CFG model is to calibrate the guidance gap 𝚫 = 𝜺 y − 𝜺 ∅ \boldsymbol{\Delta}=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{y}-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset} , since DASH’s distillation work [ 5 ] demonstrates that preserving 𝚫 \boldsymbol{\Delta} is central to generation quality. This paper shows, however, that a gap-only calibration objective admits an exact null space: there exist quantized models that achieve perfect gap fidelity—near-ideal ρ \rho and cos ⁡ ( 𝚫 ) \cos(\boldsymbol{\Delta}) scores—while the unconditional branch drifts by an unconstrained vector 𝜹 \boldsymbol{\delta} , corrupting the guided prediction at inference time. This phenomenon is termed the branch-drift trap . Unlike the training-time setting in DASH, where an explicit unconditional branch loss and hundreds of thousands of gradient steps over unfrozen weights close this null space automatically, PTQ calibrates only quantization thresholds over frozen weights in a few hundred iterations—a regime in which no gradient mechanism exists to suppress 𝜹 \boldsymbol{\delta} . To address both challenges, this paper makes four contributions. 1. CFG latency characterization : the two-pass guided-inference overhead is measured empirically on an NVIDIA T4 GPU across batch sizes and floating-point formats, revealing a consistent 1.99 × \times tax hidden by all standard efficiency proxies and diagnosing a precise software-stack root cause for the failure of commodity INT8 inference to realize theoretical speedups. 2. Null-space theorem and empirical confirmation : the branch-drift trap is proved formally—showing that gap-only PTQ calibration admits an exact null space in which guided-prediction error is unconstrained—and confirmed empirically through a controlled ablation in which the best-performing model by gap diagnostics simultaneously produces the worst sample quality of any tested configuration. 3. Guidance-Aware Mixed Precision (GAMP) : a PTQ method that calibrates on the guided prediction directly, closes the null space by construction, and allocates activation bits per layer according to their contribution to guided-output degradation—a CFG-aware sensitivity criterion that the existing single-branch mixed-precision literature does not capture. 4. Deployment guidelines : concrete recommendations for HPEC practitioners on how to report efficiency, validate PTQ calibration, and allocate activation precision for CFG diffusion deployment. II Related Work Post-training quantization for diffusion models. PTQ4DM [ 14 ] established the feasibility of diffusion PTQ by collecting multi-timestep calibration data to address time-varying activation statistics. Q-Diffusion [ 8 ] introduced skip-connection partitioning and block-wise reconstruction; for text-conditioned models it collects features from both CFG branches, but its reconstruction objective is per-block MSE on each branch independently, not the guided prediction 𝜺 ~ = 𝜺 ∅ + w ​ 𝚫 \tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}+w\boldsymbol{\Delta} . PTQD [ 9 ] modeled quantization noise as a perturbation of the diffusion SDE, proposing timestep-aware mixed-precision that targets trajectory accumulation—a complementary error source to the branch-level failure identified here. TFMQ-DM [ 10 ] , APQ-DM [ 15 ] , and TCAQ-DM [ 16 ] introduced further refinements to temporal feature maintenance and per-channel calibration. Despite these advances, no existing method calibrates against 𝜺 ~ \tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}} directly: all treat the CFG model as a single-pass unconditional network during calibration, leaving the branch-drift trap structurally unaddressed. The failure mode is architecture-agnostic—it depends only on the linear combination in ( 1 ) and applies equally to convolutional UNets and transformer-based DiT architectures. Existing per-block MSE or per-tensor reconstruction losses, even when fed with dual-branch features, remain gap-like objectives in the terminal output space: they minimize branch-wise discrepancies independently. Because no explicit coupling term constrains 𝜹 \boldsymbol{\delta} , the null space of Proposition 1 remains reachable—a constant branch offset propagates through the network and achieves low per-block error on both branches simultaneously while severely corrupting 𝜺 ~ \tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}} . Mixed-precision allocation. BRECQ [ 7 ] and HAWQ [ 11 ] allocate bit-widths by per-layer sensitivity derived from block-wise reconstruction error or Hessian curvature—single-pass proxies that do not account for CFG’s dual-branch structure. GAMP instead measures sensitivity through ‖ 𝜺 ~ l q − 𝜺 ~ l f ​ p ‖ 2 \left\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}^{q}_{l}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}^{fp}_{l}\right\|^{2} , the quantity CFG sampling depends on directly, targeting the deployment-critical failure mode rather than a reconstruction proxy. CFG distillation and the DASH null space. DASH [ 5 ] compresses a 35.8M-parameter CFG teacher to a 6.1M student via distillation, introducing ρ \rho and cos ⁡ ( 𝚫 ) \cos(\boldsymbol{\Delta}) as guidance-fidelity diagnostics and proving a training-time null space for gap matching under full gradient access. The present work extends this analysis to the PTQ regime, where frozen weights make the null space provably impossible to escape via gap calibration alone, and demonstrates that the diagnostics DASH correctly uses for distillation monitoring become insufficient —and actively misleading—as PTQ calibration objectives. III Method III-A Preliminaries At each of K = 50 K\!=\!50 DDIM [ 3 ] steps, two forward passes through the UNet yield 𝜺 y ​ ( x t , t ) \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{y}(x_{t},t) (conditional, class label y y ) and 𝜺 ∅ ​ ( x t , t ) \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}(x_{t},t) (unconditional, null token), combined by ( 1 ). The guidance gap 𝚫 = 𝜺 y − 𝜺 ∅ \boldsymbol{\Delta}=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{y}-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset} carries the class signal; DASH [ 5 ] quantifies its preservation by ρ = 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ 𝚫 q ‖ ] / 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ 𝚫 f ​ p ‖ ] \rho\!=\!\mathbb{E}[\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{q}\|]/\mathbb{E}[\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{fp}\|] (magnitude ratio; ideal 1) and cos ⁡ ( 𝚫 q , 𝚫 f ​ p ) \cos(\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{q},\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{fp}) (directional alignment; ideal 1). Quantization thresholds are optimized via AdaRound-style [ 6 ] learnable weight rounding with MSE-optimal activation clipping, over 800 iterations using 1 024 calibration images drawn uniformly from the CIFAR-10 training set; network weights are frozen throughout. Weights are quantized per-output-channel (symmetric, signed), providing scale granularity that substantially reduces clipping error at W4; activations are quantized per-tensor (asymmetric, unsigned) with MSE-optimal clipping thresholds. Biases and normalization parameters remain at FP32. Bit-operations BOPs = ∑ l M l ​ w b ​ a b \text{BOPs}\!=\!\sum_{l}M_{l}w_{b}a_{b} ( M l M_{l} : layer MACs, w b w_{b} : weight bits, a b a_{b} : activation bits) serve as the hardware-agnostic compute metric. The first and last UNet convolutions ( conv_in , conv_out ) remain FP32, consistent with standard diffusion PTQ practice [ 8 ] . III-B The Branch-Drift Trap: Null-Space Analysis The most natural PTQ calibration objective for a CFG model is to minimize the guidance-gap reconstruction error: ℒ gap = ‖ ( 𝜺 y q − 𝜺 ∅ q ) − ( 𝜺 y f ​ p − 𝜺 ∅ f ​ p ) ‖ 2 . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gap}}=\left\|(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{y}^{q}-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{q})-(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{y}^{fp}-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{fp})\right\|^{2}. (2) This is well-motivated: ℒ gap \mathcal{L}_{\text{gap}} directly penalizes drift in 𝚫 \boldsymbol{\Delta} , the quantity DASH identifies as the primary quality determinant. Yet it is provably insufficient. Proposition 1 (Null space of gap-only PTQ) . For any vector 𝛅 \boldsymbol{\delta} , the assignment 𝛆 y q = 𝛆 y f ​ p + 𝛅 \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{y}^{q}=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{y}^{fp}+\boldsymbol{\delta} and 𝛆 ∅ q = 𝛆 ∅ f ​ p + 𝛅 \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{q}=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{fp}+\boldsymbol{\delta} achieves ℒ gap = 0 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gap}}=0 , leaving the unconditional branch drift 𝛅 \boldsymbol{\delta} entirely unconstrained. Proof. ( 𝜺 y q − 𝜺 ∅ q ) = ( 𝜺 y f ​ p + 𝜹 ) − ( 𝜺 ∅ f ​ p + 𝜹 ) = 𝜺 y f ​ p − 𝜺 ∅ f ​ p (\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{y}^{q}-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{q})=(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{y}^{fp}+\boldsymbol{\delta})-(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{fp}+\boldsymbol{\delta})=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{y}^{fp}-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{fp} , so ℒ gap = 0 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gap}}=0 for any 𝜹 \boldsymbol{\delta} . ∎ The consequence for sample quality follows immediately. Proposition 2 (Guided-prediction error under null-space drift) . Under any null-space solution with drift 𝛅 \boldsymbol{\delta} : 𝜺 ~ q − 𝜺 ~ f ​ p = 𝜹 , \tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}^{q}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}^{fp}=\boldsymbol{\delta}, (3) independent of guidance scale w w and regardless of how well the gap is calibrated. Proof. Substitute 𝚫 q = 𝚫 f ​ p \boldsymbol{\Delta}^{q}\!=\!\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{fp} (Proposition 1 ) and 𝜺 ∅ q = 𝜺 ∅ f ​ p + 𝜹 \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{q}\!=\!\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{fp}+\boldsymbol{\delta} into ( 1 ): 𝜺 ~ q − 𝜺 ~ f ​ p = [ ( 𝜺 ∅ f ​ p + 𝜹 ) + w ​ 𝚫 f ​ p ] − [ 𝜺 ∅ f ​ p + w ​ 𝚫 f ​ p ] = 𝜹 \tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}^{q}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}^{fp}=[(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{fp}+\boldsymbol{\delta})+w\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{fp}]-[\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{fp}+w\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{fp}]=\boldsymbol{\delta} . ∎ Corollary 1 (Gap-fidelity metrics are insufficient) . ρ = 1 \rho\!=\!1 and cos ⁡ ( 𝚫 q , 𝚫 f ​ p ) = 1 \cos(\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{q},\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{fp})\!=\!1 are simultaneously achievable with ‖ 𝛅 ‖ ≫ 0 \left\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\right\|\gg 0 . At each of the K K DDIM steps, Proposition 2 contributes ‖ 𝛅 ‖ \left\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\right\| of per-step error; over the full trajectory, ℓ 2 \ell_{2} error accumulates as 𝒪 ⁡ ( K ​ ‖ 𝛅 ‖ ) \mathcal{O}(K\left\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\right\|) . Guidance-gap metrics are necessary but not sufficient for PTQ sample quality under CFG. PTQ provides no mechanism to suppress this drift. In DASH’s distillation setting [ 5 ] , an explicit unconditional branch loss ℒ u ​ n = ‖ 𝜺 ∅ student − 𝜺 ∅ teacher ‖ 2 \mathcal{L}_{un}\!=\!\left\|\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{\text{student}}-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}^{\text{teacher}}\right\|^{2} applied over > > 200K gradient iterations on unfrozen weights directly suppresses 𝜹 \boldsymbol{\delta} . In PTQ, threshold optimization has only 𝒪 ⁡ ( L ) \mathcal{O}(L) degrees of freedom (one clipping range per quantizable layer), and the gap loss reaches ℒ gap ≈ 0 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gap}}\!\approx\!0 trivially by shifting both branch outputs by a common offset without genuinely aligning either branch to its full-precision reference. The branch-drift trap is therefore a structural property of any gap-only PTQ objective, not an optimization pathology. At larger guidance scales ( w ∼ 7 w\!\sim\!7 –15 in text-to-image generation), the guided-prediction magnitude grows as | 𝜺 ~ | ∝ w ​ ‖ 𝚫 ‖ |\tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}|\propto w\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\| while 𝜹 \boldsymbol{\delta} remains fixed in absolute magnitude by ( 3 ), making the drift a proportionally larger directional contamination of the sampling score. The branch-drift trap is therefore expected to intensify at production guidance scales. Propositions 1 – 2 jointly imply that the PTQ objective must constrain the guided prediction 𝜺 ~ = 𝜺 ∅ + w ​ 𝚫 \tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\emptyset}+w\boldsymbol{\Delta} directly. The per-layer guided-output error is defined as: ℰ ⁡ ( l ) = ‖ 𝜺 ~ l q − 𝜺 ~ l f ​ p ‖ 2 , \mathcal{E}(l)=\left\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}^{q}_{l}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}^{fp}_{l}\right\|^{2}, (4) where l l indexes a quantizable Conv2d or Linear layer; 𝜺 ~ l q \tilde{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}^{q}_{l} is the full-network guided output when layer l l ’s quantized thresholds are active—no intermediate feature-map hooks are required. ℰ ⁡ ( l ) = 0 \mathcal{E}(l)\!=\!0 requires 𝜹 = 0 \boldsymbol{\delta}\!=\!0 , closing the null space by construction. GAMP uses ℰ ⁡ ( l ) \mathcal{E}(l) as both its per-layer sensitivity signal and the basis of its calibration objective. III-C Guidance-Aware Mixed Precision (GAMP) Activations are substantially more sensitive than weights to bit-reduction in CFG models; GAMP exploits this asymmetry by fixing all weights to 4 bits and allocating activation bits per layer, concentrating precision where the guided output is most sensitive. V Conclusion This paper characterizes post-training quantization of CFG diffusion models along three dimensions the existing literature has left unaddressed. Measured profiling on T4 confirms a consistent 1.99 × \times guided-inference overhead hidden by all standard efficiency metrics. A precise software-stack diagnosis isolates the 147 × \times INT8 slowdown to an operator-fallback artifact rather than an arithmetic limitation, clarifying that the BOPs-to-latency gap is a deployment-pipeline problem. The branch-drift trap—an exact null space in gap-only PTQ calibration, confirmed at ( cos ⁡ ( 𝚫 ) = 0.882 \cos(\boldsymbol{\Delta})\!=\!0.882 , FID 334)—is the paper’s central theoretical and empirical contribution. GAMP closes this trap by construction and allocates activation bits by guided-output sensitivity, achieving a 49% FID improvement over the uniform-spending reference at matched average precision ( b ¯ \bar{b} 6) and near-W4A8 quality at 13% fewer BOPs than the uniform W4A8 counterpart ( b ¯ \bar{b} 5). For HPEC practitioners, three guidelines follow: report guided-step BOPs; validate PTQ calibration with guided-prediction error rather than gap diagnostics alone; and allocate activation bits by GAMP sensitivity when the activation cliff falls within the compression regime. Limitations and future work. Experiments are restricted to × 32 32\!\times\!32 pixel-space diffusion (CIFAR-10) on a compact 6.1M student; validating GAMP on Stable Diffusion and similar latent CFG models, and on Hopper-generation accelerators (e.g., H100) where INT8 tensor-core support is more mature, is the primary scale-up direction. The branch-drift analysis predicts the trap intensifies with w w , motivating ablations at guidance scales w ∼ 7 w\!\sim\!7 –15 typical of text-to-image generation.
